title: The way of prayer (CCC 2663–2672)
hook: to the Father, through Jesus, in the Spirit

segments.voice: Yesterday, where prayer comes from: the word, the liturgy, faith, hope, charity, and today. Your line was today is a source. What ordinary moment turned into a place to start? Day one thousand one hundred forty-three.

An old paper letter needed three things to arrive. A name on the front: who it's for. A stamp and a carrier: how it travels. And something inside that made it worth sending at all. Get one wrong and the letter sits in a sorting room forever. Catholic prayer has a shape like that, and it's hiding in plain sight. Listen to the endings of the prayers at Mass and the same little pattern keeps turning up: to someone, through someone, in someone. Three small words. The Catechism lays them out as the way prayer travels. Today: the way of prayer.
screen: `WHO IT'S FOR.` → `HOW IT TRAVELS.` → `TO, THROUGH, IN.`

segments.voice: Start with to. In Catholic teaching, prayer is addressed above all to the Father. Jesus says so at the Last Supper, in the Douay-Rheims: "if you ask the Father any thing in my name, he will give it you." Notice the second half of that sentence: in my name. That's through. The Catechism says there's no other way of Christian prayer than Christ. Whether it's said alone or together, aloud or silently, it reaches the Father through Jesus. But Jesus isn't only the road. He's also someone people pray to directly, by name. Paul writes "That in the name of Jesus every knee should bow." The Catechism describes a prayer from the Christian East, often called the Jesus Prayer, which joins his name to a plea for mercy and is repeated slowly, again and again. It calls calling on his name the simplest way of praying always. Then in. Paul admits something honest: "we know not what we should pray for as we ought; but the Spirit himself asketh for us with unspeakable groanings." When words run out, Catholics say, the Spirit is praying inside the one who prays. So the Church invites people to call on the Spirit too, every day, with the old words "Come, Holy Spirit," especially at the start and the end of something important. To the Father. Through the Son. In the Spirit. Catholics hold this as one God, not three, and the prayer moves the way they believe God does.
screen: `TO THE FATHER.` · `THROUGH JESUS, IN HIS NAME.` · `TO JESUS, BY NAME.` · `IN THE SPIRIT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray to each person once. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, you can turn first to the Father, with one short line of your own: thanks, or a need. Then say the name of Jesus slowly, once, and let it sit. Then the old words, "Come, Holy Spirit," and wait in the quiet after them. If you don't pray, you can simply notice three directions: what's above you, what's beside you, and what's within. The bell holds the time.
The way of prayer. In Catholic teaching, prayer goes to the Father, through Jesus and in his name, in the Holy Spirit. Today's words.
Your line: to, through, in. Today, the next time you start or finish something that matters, try the three short words from today: Come, Holy Spirit. Day one thousand one hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Catholic liturgical prayers are usually addressed to the Father and close through Christ in the Holy Spirit; many Catholics also pray directly to Jesus, some with the Jesus Prayer, and call on the Holy Spirit before important work.

original.note: Latin: come, Holy Spirit — the old opening words the Church uses to call on the Spirit.

trapdoor: what you thought: prayer is talking to God, and that's all there is to its shape.
what it means: in Catholic teaching prayer goes to the Father, through Jesus, in the Spirit, and people also pray to Jesus and to the Spirit directly.
what a scholar hears: the pattern follows John 16:23 and Romans 8:26, and it echoes the way Catholic liturgical prayers close: through Christ, in the unity of the Holy Spirit.
recall: a firm habit of doing good

notes: CCC 2663–2672 paraphrased (copyrighted English). Check: 'no other way of Christian prayer than Christ' (2664), the Jesus Prayer described (2667), invocation of the name as the simplest way of praying always (2668), the invitation to call on the Spirit every day, especially at the start and end of important actions (2670–2671).
Hook: 'the same little pattern keeps turning up' in the endings of prayers at Mass refers to the conclusion of the collects; confirm the description is fair.
'Come, Holy Spirit' is said aloud as the traditional opening words, not a new prayer; the Latin original is given as Veni, Sancte Spiritus (the opening of the sequence and of the antiphon). Confirm.
Douay-Rheims: confirm exact wording of John 16:23, Philippians 2:10 and Romans 8:26.
Fork setup places John 16:23 at the Last Supper (John 13–17); confirm.
